overview.title: Spider-Man, decade by decade
overview.lede: Spider-Man is the character Marvel keeps having to re-solve, because the premise has a clock in it: a teenager whose problem is that he is a teenager. Let him age and you lose it; freeze him and the book stops moving. Sixty years of this shelf is sixty years of people trying to answer that, and the answers — marry him off, clone him, restart him in a parallel universe, replace him — are where all the famous arguments come from.

sections.h: Ditko: the strangest-looking book Marvel published
body: The idea was Stan Lee's and the execution was Steve Ditko's, and it is worth being blunt about how much of it is Ditko: he plotted the book outright from around #25 and took a credit for it, and the things people love about early Spider-Man — the anxiety, the ordinariness, the sense that Peter's real problem is rent and Aunt May rather than a supervillain — are his sensibility, not the house one.

Look at how unglamorous it is. Ditko draws a skinny, awkward kid with bad posture in a New York of fire escapes and small rooms. His villains are wrong-looking on purpose — a man with a fishbowl on his head, a man with mechanical arms and a bowl haircut — and his Spider-Man moves like an insect rather than like an athlete, crouched and folded into corners.

The high point everyone points at is #33, where Spider-Man is pinned under collapsed machinery and lifts it. Ditko gives it several pages of near silence and shifting camera, and it still teaches the lesson every later artist learned from it: the drama is the effort, not the punch.
Ditko left after #38 in 1966, after communication with Lee had broken down entirely. Reportedly they were not speaking by the end.

fig.cap: Left: #1, 1963. Right: #33 — the machinery sequence, and the reason Ditko is on every artist's list.

makers.b: Watch the body language. Ditko's Spider-Man is almost never standing up straight; he crouches, coils, hangs upside down and folds his limbs into the panel. Nobody else at Marvel was drawing a hero who looked physically uncomfortable, and it is exactly right for the character.

sections.h: Romita Sr. makes him handsome, and the book becomes a soap opera
body: John Romita Sr. came off romance comics, and it shows immediately and deliberately. Peter gets a jawline. The girls get real faces. The book stops being about a nervous kid and becomes about a college student with two women interested in him, and within a year it was Marvel's best-selling title.

The single most famous panel of the transition is the last page of #42, where Mary Jane finally turns around: Face it, tiger — you just hit the jackpot. That is a romance-comic beat, staged like one, and it is the moment the series' engine changes from anxiety to romance.

What is lost is worth naming too. Romita's villains are cleaner and less strange than Ditko's — the Rhino, the Shocker, the Kingpin are wonderfully designed and none of them is uncanny the way the Vulture and Doctor Octopus were.

Gil Kane arrives at the end of this stretch, and he is the other name to know. #96–98 in 1971 are the anti-drug issues that Marvel published without the Comics Code seal after the Code refused to approve them for depicting drug use at all — the Code was rewritten shortly afterwards. The book had genuine cultural weight by this point.

fig.cap: Left: #42, the Mary Jane reveal. Right: #50, Spider-Man No More — a costume in a bin and a man walking away, which is one of the most copied images in comics.

makers.b: Look at the faces in the crowd scenes. Romita gives every background character a specific, readable expression, which is a romance-comic discipline — and it is what makes Peter's world feel populated rather than staged.

Kane draws impact better than almost anyone. Low angles, figures thrown out of frame, and a habit of putting the camera under a punch so you feel the recoil. Todd McFarlane's line about him — that when he hit somebody it felt like you were being shot out of a cannon — is exactly the thing to watch for.

sections.h: The issue where the Silver Age ends
body: #121, 1973. The Green Goblin throws Gwen Stacy off a bridge and Spider-Man catches her with a webline, and the snap that saves her is what kills her. Gerry Conway wrote it and Gil Kane drew it, and it is routinely cited as the moment the Silver Age of superhero comics ends — the point at which the hero could arrive in time and still lose.

The famous detail is a single sound effect. There is a small snap lettered at Gwen's neck as the web catches her, and the comic never explains it. Readers have been arguing about whether Spider-Man killed her since 1973, which is precisely the argument the story wants.

Conway and Ross Andru then run the book for four years, and the second thing they leave behind is #129 and the Punisher — a killer introduced as an antagonist who was immediately more popular than the plot required. Andru is the shelf's most underrated draughtsman: his New York is architecturally real, and he stages Spider-Man in it rather than in front of it.

fig.cap: Left: #121 — the cover is a row of faces and the words Turning Point, which is the whole marketing. Right: #129, and Andru puts the Punisher in the foreground on a rooftop like a crime paperback.

sections.h: Roger Stern, and the most perfectly built run on the book
body: Roger Stern's stretch is short — a couple of dozen issues — and it has a reputation out of all proportion to its length. Three of the stories in it turn up on more or less every best-Spider-Man list ever compiled: Nothing Can Stop the Juggernaut (#229–230), the Hobgoblin's arrival (#238), and The Kid Who Collects Spider-Man (#248).

That last one is the argument for Stern in a single issue. Spider-Man visits a boy who has an enormous scrapbook about him, tells him his secret identity, and then the last page tells you why. It is eleven pages long, it has no fight in it, and people have been recommending it for forty years.
John Romita Jr. is the artist for most of it, in his early, cleaner manner — before the blocky, heavy-shadow style of his later career. John Byrne and Mike Zeck pass through as well.

fig.cap: Left: #238, the Hobgoblin. Right: #248 — a kid in a bedroom holding a scrapbook. That is the cover, and it is the best-loved single issue on this shelf.

sections.h: McFarlane, Venom, and the invention of the superstar artist
body: Todd McFarlane arrives on Amazing in 1988 and changes what a mainstream superhero comic is allowed to look like. The webbing goes from neat parallel lines to a mad scribble; the poses become impossible; Spider-Man starts being drawn as something that folds, with knees above his ears and fingers splayed like a spider's legs. It is not anatomically defensible and it is completely convincing.

#300 gives Venom his full debut, and Venom is the character that made the 1990s possible — a villain designed as a dark mirror with too many teeth, who was immediately more marketable than most of Marvel's heroes.

Then the industry's centre of gravity moves. In 1990 Marvel gives McFarlane his own title to write and draw, and Spider-Man #1 sold in numbers no comic had sold before — over two million copies, on the strength of an artist's name on the cover. Two years later he and six others left to found Image. This shelf holds the book that proved it could be done.
Erik Larsen follows him on Amazing and is the useful comparison: same era, same writer, and a much more Kirby-descended sense of weight and impact where McFarlane is all silhouette and texture.

fig.cap: Left: #300, Venom. Right: Spider-Man #1, 1990 — look at how much of that cover is webbing. The drawing is the product.

quote.t: Gil Kane was a guy who when he hit somebody, bam, it felt like you were getting shot out of a cannon. George Pérez, he would draw machinery that still to this day stuns me.

makers.b: Two signatures. The webbing, which he draws as a tangled organic mess rather than a grid — it eats whole panels and it is why his pages read as texture first. And the silhouette: he contorts Spider-Man into shapes a person cannot make, because the shape reads faster than the anatomy.

sections.h: The Clone Saga, and the book that was published against it
body: For two years the four Spider-Man titles ran one interlocking story built on a single unbearable idea: the Peter Parker you had been reading since 1962 was the clone, and the real one had been away. It is the most notorious storyline in the character's history, it ran roughly four times longer than anyone intended, and it is the standard example of a plot that changed course so often it stopped meaning anything.

It is worth reading anyway, and this shelf lets you, because the failure is instructive and because Ben Reilly is genuinely good — the one thing nearly everyone agrees on is that the replacement Spider-Man was better written than the story he was in.

The counter-programming is the sleeper of this whole shelf. While that was going on, Kurt Busiek and Pat Olliffe were quietly publishing Untold Tales of Spider-Man — brand-new stories slotted into the gaps between the Lee/Ditko issues, at 99 cents, with no continuity baggage at all. Read the two side by side and you have the 1990s argument in miniature.

fig.cap: Left: #400 — a gravestone, foil, and A Death in the Family. Right: Untold Tales #1, drawn to look like 1964 on purpose.

sections.h: Two answers to the ageing problem at once
body: Marvel solved the clock problem twice in the same five years, in opposite directions.

Ultimate Spider-Man started him over: fifteen years old again, in 2000, with no continuity behind him. Brian Michael Bendis wrote it in long conversational scenes — the first issue takes seven pages to get to the spider bite — and Mark Bagley drew 111 consecutive issues, which broke Lee and Kirby's 102-issue record on Fantastic Four and is still the longest unbroken creative team Marvel has had.

J. Michael Straczynski and John Romita Jr. took the opposite route on the real book: keep the forty years, and dig underneath them. The totem arc asks whether the spider bite was ever the explanation at all, and Aunt May finding out is the best-regarded single scene of the modern era.

Romita Jr. by now is a different artist from the one in the Stern volume — blockier, heavier, everything built from slabs and hard black shadow. Comparing his two runs on this shelf is the clearest thirty-year artist study available anywhere on the site.

fig.cap: Left: Ultimate Spider-Man #1. Right: Romita Jr.'s first JMS issue — compare the weight of that figure with his #248 twenty years earlier.

body: Death of Ultimate Spider-Man does the thing the main line structurally cannot: it lets him die, at sixteen, having been Spider-Man for eleven years of publishing, and then hands the costume to Miles Morales rather than resetting.

It works because Bendis and Bagley had spent a decade earning it. Nothing else on this shelf gets to have a real ending — and that is not a complaint about the main books, it is the structural fact the whole tour has been circling.

fig.cap: A spider on black. No figure, no title character.

tone.sub: Sixteen books, and they are not variations on one comic. If you want a particular flavour of Spider-Man, here is where it lives.

modes.b: Ditko's New York — a nervous kid, uncanny villains, and a hero who crouches. The furthest from the modern character and the most distinctive book on the shelf.
Romita Sr.'s soap opera. College, two women, a supporting cast with faces. This is the Spider-Man most people carry in their head.
The Conway years, and the bridge. The book learns that the hero can do everything right and lose anyway, and it never fully recovers.
Stern's run — short, and story for story the most consistently excellent stretch anyone has written. Start here if you want proof the character works.
Busiek and Olliffe writing new 1964 comics in 1995. No angst, no continuity to know, and a real fondness for the material it is imitating.
Art as the product. Impossible poses, webbing everywhere, Venom on every other cover, and a book that sold two million copies on a signature.
The Clone Saga. Read it as a document of what happens when a story is not allowed to end — and for Ben Reilly, who deserved better.
Decompressed, conversational, built for the trade paperback. Two very different answers to how you make a sixty-year-old character legible again.
The only book here that gets to finish, and the reason Miles Morales exists.

asm-o1.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus Vol. 1
asm-o1.lede: The Lee and Ditko run, which is stranger, sadder and more idiosyncratic than its reputation — and much more Ditko's book than the credits box suggests.

sections.h: How much of this is Ditko
body: By around #25 Ditko was plotting the book outright and took a plotting credit for it, and the features that define early Spider-Man are his. The ordinariness — rent, Aunt May's health, a job Peter needs — is a Ditko preoccupation, not a house style, and no other Marvel book of the period is built on it.

His visual register is unique in the line. Peter is skinny and badly postured; the villains are wrong rather than imposing; and Spider-Man himself is drawn as something that folds into corners and hangs upside down rather than as an athlete.
The set-piece is #33, pinned under machinery in a flooding room. It runs on near-silence and a slowly pulling-back camera, and it is still the standard example of drawing effort rather than action.

makers.b: Look at the hands. Ditko's fingers are long, splayed and constantly doing something — gripping walls, pointing, curling in anxiety. It is the most expressive part of his figure drawing and nobody else in 1963 was using hands that way.

fig.cap: Left: #1, 1963 — note the Fantastic Four are on the cover, because a new title needed the help. Right: #33.

body: One of the small handful of Silver Age runs that is genuinely still read for pleasure rather than for history, and the consensus is that it gets better as it goes — the first ten issues are finding their feet, and by the twenties the book is extraordinary.

The other consistent line, and it has grown louder over the decades, is that Ditko is under-credited. Once you know he was plotting it, the run reads differently, and the drop in strangeness the moment he leaves is the strongest evidence.

asm-o2.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus Vol. 2
asm-o2.lede: Romita Sr. takes over and the best-selling superhero comic in America turns into a romance book with fights in it.

body: Romita came off romance comics and applied that training directly. Peter gets handsome, the cast gets glamorous, and the emotional engine changes from anxiety to who is going out with whom. Within about a year Amazing was Marvel's top seller.

The moment is the last page of #42, Mary Jane in the doorway. It is staged exactly like a romance-comic reveal — held back for two years of publishing, then delivered as a full-figure panel with one line of dialogue.
#50 is the other keeper: Spider-Man No More!, a costume in a rubbish bin, and the debut of the Kingpin. That cover has been re-staged for every superhero at Marvel at least once.

makers.b: Watch the storytelling clarity. Romita stages every scene so you can read it at a glance — clean silhouettes, one clear focal point, faces angled to camera. It is commercial art at a very high level and it is why the book's sales moved.

fig.cap: Left: #42. Right: #50 — the most imitated composition on this shelf.

body: Beloved, and the site of the shelf's oldest argument: Ditko or Romita. Both camps are large and both are right about something — Romita's Spider-Man is warmer, better drawn as pure craft, and vastly more popular; Ditko's is stranger and more personal.

The criticism you will see of this stretch is that the villains get safer. The Rhino and the Shocker are terrific designs and neither is unsettling in the way Ditko's were. What replaces the strangeness is a supporting cast good enough to carry sixty years.

asm-o3.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus Vol. 3
asm-o3.lede: The end of the Lee era, Gil Kane's arrival, and the three issues that forced the Comics Code to rewrite itself.

body: The US Department of Health, Education and Welfare asked Marvel for an anti-drug story. Stan Lee wrote one, and the Comics Code refused to approve it — the Code as written forbade depicting drugs at all, regardless of what the story said about them. Marvel published the three issues without the seal. Nothing happened, everyone noticed, and the Code was revised shortly afterwards.
It is a genuinely important moment in the medium's history and the issues themselves are decent rather than great, which is worth knowing going in.
Artistically the story here is Gil Kane, arriving to take the book off Romita, bringing a much more violent, low-angle sense of physical impact.

makers.b: Look for the upshot — Kane puts the camera below the action constantly, so figures loom and punches come at you. He also throws bodies clean out of the panel border. This is the technique McFarlane meant about being shot out of a cannon.

fig.cap: #96. Note the top-right corner: no Comics Code seal, where every other Marvel comic on the rack that month had one.

body: Rated a notch below the two volumes either side of it as pure reading, and well ahead of them as history. The drug issues are the reason people buy it, and readers routinely report being slightly underwhelmed by them as stories — the significance is the publishing act, not the script.
What is genuinely undervalued here is the art transition. Watching Kane take a Romita book and make it violent is one of the more interesting handovers on the shelf.

asm-o4.title: Amazing Spider-Man Omnibus Vol. 4
asm-o4.lede: Gwen Stacy dies, the Punisher arrives, and superhero comics stop being able to promise that the hero gets there in time.

body: Gerry Conway was in his early twenties when he wrote it. The Goblin throws Gwen off a bridge; Spider-Man catches her with a web; there is a small snap lettered beside her neck, and she is dead when he pulls her up.

The refusal to explain that sound effect is the craft. The comic never tells you whether the fall killed her or the rescue did, and fifty years of readers have argued about it — which is a far more disturbing outcome than either answer would have been.
It is very widely treated as the end of the Silver Age. Before it, a superhero who arrived in time won.

#129 introduces Frank Castle as an antagonist and he is instantly more interesting than his role — a 1970s vigilante-thriller character walking into a superhero book, at exactly the moment the audience wanted one.

Ross Andru draws four years of this and is the most under-appreciated artist on the shelf. His New York has real architecture and real depth; he stages Spider-Man within the city rather than posed in front of it, and his aerial webswinging shots are the template everyone still uses.

fig.cap: Left: #121. Right: #129 — Andru's rooftop, and a villain who reads as a crime-novel cover.

body: #121–122 is on essentially every best-Spider-Man-story list ever assembled, and its status as a turning point for the whole medium is about as settled as these things get.

The volume around it gets a quieter reception. Conway's four years are generally rated solid rather than special, and the frequent note is that the book spends a while unsure what to do with a hero it has just traumatised. Andru is the thing readers consistently say they came away newly impressed by.

utsm-o1.title: Untold Tales of Spider-Man Omnibus
utsm-o1.lede: New comics written in 1995 and set inside 1963, at 99 cents, while the Clone Saga was happening in the room next door. The shelf's biggest sleeper.

body: Kurt Busiek pitched a book with no continuity requirement at all: stories slotted into the gaps between existing Lee/Ditko issues, so a new reader could start anywhere and a long-time reader got the pleasure of watching the seams line up.

It arrived in the middle of the Clone Saga, priced at 99 cents, and it is impossible not to read it as an argument — here is the character with no baggage, no crossover and no reveal, and it is still good.

Pat Olliffe draws it in a deliberately period register: clean lines, readable staging, a Peter who looks fifteen. Not pastiche exactly — the storytelling is modern — but it is set-dressed to 1964 with real care.

fig.cap: Olliffe's #1, drawn to sit on a rack in 1964 and to be legible to someone who has never read a comic.

body: Consistently described as underrated and better than it needed to be, and it is one of the books long-time Spider-Man readers recommend to people who bounced off the modern character.

It sold modestly and was cancelled, which is the usual fate of a book positioned as an alternative rather than an event. Its reputation has only gone up since. The reservation, such as it is: nothing in it can matter — the stories are wedged between issues whose outcomes are already printed — so it trades stakes for charm on purpose.

stern-o1.title: Spider-Man by Roger Stern Omnibus
stern-o1.lede: The shortest great run on the character, and story for story the best-made comics on this shelf.

sections.h: Three stories that are on every list
body: Nothing Can Stop the Juggernaut (#229–230) is the purest Spider-Man story ever built: an opponent he genuinely cannot beat, two issues of him failing to beat him anyway, and a win that comes from persistence rather than power.

The Hobgoblin (#238 onward) is the best-executed mystery in the character's history. Stern seeded a real identity, laid fair clues, and then left the book before the reveal — which later writers resolved differently, and which is the great what-if of this shelf.
The Kid Who Collects Spider-Man (#248) is eleven pages, has no fight in it, and is the single most recommended issue on the whole site. Read it cold. Do not look up what happens.

makers.b: This is early Romita Jr. — cleaner, lighter and closer to his father than the blocky, black-heavy style he is now known for. Put it next to his JMS work on this same shelf; it is the clearest long-range artist study available here.

fig.cap: Left: the Hobgoblin's arrival. Right: #248, whose cover is a boy holding a scrapbook.

body: Stern is very widely named the best Spider-Man writer after Lee, and this run is the reason. Reader polls routinely place three separate stories from it in the character's all-time top ten, which no other run manages.

The only real complaint is that it is unfinished — Stern left before resolving the Hobgoblin, and the eventual answer given by other hands is not the one he had planned. He returned to tell his version much later, and readers still argue about which counts.
If you read exactly one book on this shelf, this is the recommendation.

mcf-o1.title: ASM by Michelinie & McFarlane Omnibus
mcf-o1.lede: Venom's debut, and the year a penciller became bigger than the character he was drawing.

body: Two things, and both are still in use. The webbing: he abandoned the neat ruled grid every artist had drawn since 1962 and replaced it with a tangled organic scribble that eats whole panels. And the silhouette: he contorts Spider-Man into shapes a human spine will not make, on the principle that the shape reads faster than the anatomy.

#300 is the full debut of Venom, and it is hard to overstate how much that design mattered commercially. A black mirror-image with a rictus grin and too many teeth, arriving exactly when the audience wanted something harder-edged.

David Michelinie is the writer for all of it and gets somewhat lost in the discussion, which is unfair — the Venom concept is substantially his, and he keeps a genuinely warm Peter Parker underneath the art.

fig.cap: Left: #300. Right: #316 — the tongue, the teeth and the impossible pose, all doing exactly what they were designed to.

body: One of the most commercially significant runs Marvel ever published, and the reception splits cleanly along a line that has not moved in thirty-five years: McFarlane's art is either the most exciting thing that ever happened to the book or the moment it went wrong.
What is not much argued about is that the writing is decent and conventional, and that #300 is a genuine landmark — among the most sought-after modern back issues in existence.
The cover scan on this tile is one of the shelf's low-resolution ones; that is all the Marvel Database holds.

larsen-o1.title: Spider-Man by Michelinie & Larsen Omnibus
larsen-o1.lede: Same writer, same era, a completely different artist — which makes this the most useful comparison book on the shelf.

body: Erik Larsen follows McFarlane on Amazing with David Michelinie still writing, so almost everything is held constant except the pencils. That is a rare experiment to be able to run.

Larsen's lineage is Kirby: weight, impact, figures that are solid objects colliding. McFarlane's is texture and silhouette. Put #316 and any Larsen fight scene side by side and you can see two entirely different theories of what a punch is.
Larsen also leans harder into the goofy end of the rogues gallery, which suits him — his monsters are funny and enormous in a way McFarlane's brooding never was.

fig.cap: Larsen's Spider-Man is heavier and more grounded than McFarlane's, and the villains take up more of the frame.

body: Warmly regarded and not much argued about. Larsen has a real following — largely from Savage Dragon, which he has drawn single-handed for over thirty years — and readers who find McFarlane's work airless tend to prefer this.

The common note is that it is the least essential of the three McFarlane-era volumes and the most purely enjoyable. It also overlaps the other two by design; several issues here are also in the Michelinie & McFarlane and vs. Venom books, and marking them once marks them everywhere.

mcf-o2.title: Spider-Man by Todd McFarlane Omnibus
mcf-o2.lede: The best-selling comic book ever printed, and a document of the exact moment the industry decided the artist was the product.

body: Marvel gave McFarlane an adjectiveless Spider-Man title to write and draw himself, launched it with multiple covers, and it sold in numbers no comic had reached before — over two million copies of #1. Not on the strength of a story anybody could describe. On the strength of a name.

That is the historical significance, and it is worth being clear-eyed about the comics themselves: Torment, the opening arc, is famous for atmosphere, repetition and a great deal of doom doom doom lettering, and light on plot. McFarlane was a spectacular draughtsman and a novice writer, and the book shows both.
Two years later he and six other artists left to found Image Comics. This volume is the proof of concept that made that possible.

fig.cap: #1, 1990. Count how much of the image is webbing rather than figure — the texture is the selling point.

body: Enormously important and not, on the whole, well loved. The standard assessment is that the art is extraordinary and the writing is thin — Torment in particular gets cited for mood over substance and for lettering tics that have not aged gracefully.

Its defenders point out, fairly, that atmosphere was the point and that the book is doing something genuinely unusual for a 1990 superhero comic. Its detractors point out that it is thirty pages of running through a swamp.
Either way it belongs on the shelf: this is the single most commercially consequential Spider-Man comic ever published.

vs-venom-o1.title: Spider-Man vs. Venom Omnibus
vs-venom-o1.lede: A decade of one relationship, assembled as a chronology rather than a run — the black costume's arrival through Maximum Carnage.

body: It starts with the black costume in 1984, which arrived out of Secret Wars as a design change and turned into the best long-form idea of the era: the suit is alive, it does not want to leave, and getting rid of it creates something that hates him personally.

Reading it in this order rather than by run is genuinely clarifying. Venom's escalation from horror antagonist to anti-hero with his own titles happens in about four years, and laid out chronologically you can watch the commercial pressure doing it in real time.
It ends on Maximum Carnage, which runs straight into the Clone Saga — which is why this book sits after the McFarlane volume on the shelf rather than before it.

Judged mostly as a collection decision rather than a run, and on that basis it does well: the chronology is the right one, and having the black-suit material and the Venom escalation in a single volume is genuinely useful.

The reservations are the ones any chronology book attracts — it doubles back over the two Michelinie volumes (eight issues are in both, and marking them here marks them there), and the quality swings a good deal across ten years and a dozen creative teams. The late Carnage material is generally rated the weakest part.

clone-o1.title: Spider-Man: Clone Saga Omnibus Vol. 1
clone-o1.lede: The most notorious storyline in the character's history, from the top. It is worth reading, and it is worth knowing what you are reading.

sections.h: How it was supposed to go
body: The plan was a short arc: a clone from a 1970s story returns, Peter has an identity crisis, it resolves. Sales went up, so it was extended. And extended. The full thing ran roughly two years across four monthly titles, and the central reveal — that the Peter Parker readers had followed since 1962 was the clone — was reversed, reinstated and reversed again as editorial changed its mind in public.
Reading it in a book is a very different experience from reading it monthly, and genuinely fairer to it. The four titles interlock properly here, which they manifestly did not on the rack.

The consistent bright spot is Ben Reilly. The replacement Spider-Man is written with real warmth — a man who has been away for five years and is delighted to be back — and he is far better than the machinery around him.

fig.cap: #400. A gravestone, a foil cover, and A Death in the Family — the Aunt May issue, which is one of the era's genuinely good ones and was later undone.

body: The standard shorthand for a story that went wrong, and the criticisms are specific rather than vague: it ran far longer than it was ever plotted to, it required four books a month to follow, the mystery villains (Judas Traveller, Scrier) resolved to very little, and the central premise told readers that the character they had followed for thirty years was a fake.

There is a real revisionist case, and it has been gathering strength: read collected, with the crossovers in order, the early stretch is much more coherent than its reputation, and Ben Reilly is genuinely good. Nobody argues the whole thing works.
Worth knowing before you start: the material in this volume is the part most readers rate highest. It gets harder from here.

clone-o2.title: Spider-Man: Clone Saga Omnibus Vol. 2
clone-o2.lede: The middle, where the story stops being about identity and starts being about publishing.

body: This is the densest stretch — four books a month passing the plot back and forth, which is why the chapters here are cut as Part N blocks rather than per series: reading it by title would give you one-issue chapters and no story.
Maximum Clonage is the point most readers name as the wheels coming off: more clones, a villain version, and an escalation that no longer connects to the human question the saga opened with.
It is also where the era's visual identity is most itself — the cross-hatching, the pouches, the enormous shoulders. If you want to know what 1995 looked like at Marvel, this is the volume.

Widely treated as the weakest stretch of an already contentious story, and the reasons given are consistent: too many clones, a proliferation of plot threads nobody was tracking, and the sense that the story was being extended rather than told.

Even readers making the revisionist case for the Clone Saga tend to exempt this part of it. Its defenders are mostly defending the craft — some very good artists were working very hard here — rather than the story.
Read it if you are reading the whole thing. Do not start here.

ben-o1.title: Spider-Man: Ben Reilly Omnibus Vol. 1
ben-o1.lede: The year Marvel actually did it: Peter Parker walked away and somebody else was Spider-Man in every book.

body: For about a year the line committed completely. Peter retired, Ben Reilly put on a new costume, and the four titles carried on as if this were now normal — which is a much bolder publishing act than it usually gets credit for.

And the character carries it. Ben is lighter than Peter: no guilt engine, no fifteen years of loss, genuinely happy to be doing this. Writers found him easy to write, and the books briefly relax in a way Amazing had not since the 1970s.
It ends, of course, and the ending is the thing everyone remembers rather than the year that preceded it — which is the injustice this volume corrects.

The most consistent revisionist position on the whole Clone Saga is that Ben Reilly was good and deserved better, and this volume is where the argument lives. Readers who disliked everything around it will still defend the character.

The criticism is structural rather than about him: everyone knew it would be undone, and a year of stories with a foregone conclusion is a hard sell in hindsight. The Scarlet Spider costume — a hoodie over the suit — has meanwhile become genuinely beloved, which is not what anyone predicted in 1995.

jms-o1.title: Amazing Spider-Man by J. Michael Straczynski Omnibus
jms-o1.lede: A television writer takes the main book, asks whether the spider bite was ever the explanation, and gets four excellent years and one very bad decision.

sections.h: The totem question, and Aunt May
body: J. Michael Straczynski came from Babylon 5 and brought long-arc television structure with him. His opening move is the best one anybody has made on the character in decades: what if the radioactive spider was not the cause but the occasion — what if there is an older, stranger explanation?
It is a genuinely destabilising idea and it is handled without wrecking anything, which is the difficult part.

The other thing everyone names is Aunt May finding out. Forty years of the book had treated that as the one thing that could never happen; JMS lets it happen and then writes the conversation, and it is the best-regarded scene of the modern era.
John Romita Jr. draws the bulk of it, in his mature manner — heavy black shadow, blocky construction, everything built from slabs. Compare it with his Stern-era work on this same shelf.

The volume ends with Sins Past, which retroactively gives Gwen Stacy secret children fathered by Norman Osborn. It is one of the most disliked Spider-Man stories ever published, and unusually the writer agrees: JMS has said publicly that it is his biggest regret, that his original version was different, and that it was changed on him.
It is included here because the volume collects the run, and because knowing it is coming is better than being surprised by it.

fig.cap: Left: Romita Jr.'s first issue of the run. Right: the start of Sins Past.

body: The first half is very highly regarded — commonly named the best Amazing Spider-Man since Stern, with the Romita Jr. issues singled out and the Aunt May revelation treated as a landmark.
Sins Past is the break, and readers describe it as the point the run stops being trusted. That the writer publicly disowns it is unusual and worth weighing.

Beyond this volume the run continues into One More Day, which is the most disliked Spider-Man story of all and which JMS has said was not his. None of that is collected here, so this book gets to end before the worst of it.

ult-o1.title: Ultimate Spider-Man Omnibus Vol. 1
ult-o1.lede: Start him over at fifteen with no continuity, tell it slowly, and let one artist draw all of it. It worked better than anyone expected.

body: The first issue takes seven pages to get to the spider bite and about six issues to get through the origin. In 2000 that was radical, and it is the clearest example on the site of what people mean by decompressed storytelling — scenes given room, dialogue doing the work, the whole thing paced for a collected edition rather than for a monthly.
Bendis writes teenagers better than almost anyone in comics: overlapping, repetitive, funny, and unbearably self-conscious. It is why the book outlived the line it was launched to sell.

Mark Bagley drew 111 consecutive issues of it — breaking Lee and Kirby's 102-issue record on Fantastic Four, and still the longest unbroken creative team Marvel has had. The consistency is a large part of why the run reads like a single novel.

makers.b: Watch the acting in quiet scenes. Bendis writes pages of two teenagers talking, and Bagley has to make that visually interesting with body language alone — slouches, shrugs, eye lines. It is the least showy hard job on this shelf.

fig.cap: #1, 2000. A modern rooftop, a modern skyline, and a costume that reads as fabric.

body: One of the most successful reinventions in superhero comics, and generally credited with proving that a legacy character could be restarted without being cheapened. Its DNA is visible in most Spider-Man screen adaptations since.

The criticism, where it exists, is about pace: readers who prefer a self-contained issue find the early arcs slow, and the phrase six issues to do what Lee did in eleven pages comes up. That is a fair description and a matter of taste rather than a flaw.
It is also the most straightforwardly recommendable book on this shelf for someone who has never read a comic.

ult-death-o1.title: Death of Ultimate Spider-Man Omnibus
ult-death-o1.lede: The only book on this shelf that gets a real ending, and the one that produced Miles Morales.

body: Eleven years of publishing, one continuous creative team for most of it, and then he dies at sixteen — and stays dead, which the main line is structurally unable to do.
It lands because of the decade underneath it. The supporting cast are people you have watched grow up, and the story is largely about them.
Then Miles Morales takes the costume, which at the time was a real publishing risk and is now simply one of Marvel's most valuable characters. This volume is where he starts.

fig.cap: A red spider on black. No figure, no title character — the cover tells you what has happened before you open it.

body: Treated as a rare superhero death that earned its ending, largely because it was allowed to stand and because a decade of consistent storytelling had built to it. The issues immediately following, dealing with the fallout, are often rated higher than the death itself.
The main criticism is one the book cannot help: it is an ending inside a line that continued, and the Ultimate universe's later direction complicates it somewhat.
Its real legacy is Miles — introduced here, and by some distance the most successful new Marvel character of the last twenty years.
